state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it in terms of a line of people standing on a field. If we double the distance between each person, the range (or the distance from the first person to the last person) would definitely change. So, Tom's idea that cutting the plants in half wouldn't change the range doesn't quite match up with what we know about proportionality.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I see what you mean about the people in a line. So if we cut the heights in half, the range would actually change because the difference between the tallest and shortest would be smaller. But I'm still confused about Katie's idea. If we just add \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) to each plant, how does that change the range?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think of it like a group of students lining up for a race. If each student takes a step forward, the range of the line (the distance from the first student to the last student) will still change, just like how adding \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) to each plant would change the range of their heights. So, Katie's idea also doesn't quite match up with the concept of proportionality.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it a bit better now! So if we add \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) to each plant, it actually changes the range because the tallest and shortest plants are both getting taller, right? But I'm still a bit confused about why cutting everything in half is different from adding to it. Can you explain that part again?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming addition changes range, when it doesn't) and uses confusing analogies that don't map to the mathematical concepts, resulting in the student becoming more confused rather than correcting their misconception.
score.justification_pass2: While the teacher uses concrete analogies (people in a line, students at a race), these analogies are mathematically incorrect—they misrepresent how range behaves under addition versus multiplication, leading to wrong conclusions that contradict the mathematical reality that adding a constant preserves range while scaling changes it.
